power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

info.title: Developing Effective GenAI Users: The Missing Motivational System and Why It Matters for Equity

author.affiliation: Project for Educational Research That Scales (PERTS)

text.text: Research on Generative AI (GenAI) in education has largely focused on how much students use it and its impact on learning.
This framing overlooks the motivational processes driving students' choices.
We propose broadening research to include the study of what cultures, contexts, and learning experiences give students the knowledge, skills, beliefs, and motivation to become effective GenAI users.

We define effective GenAI use and propose a motivational model of how learning environments and students' perceptions of them shape their goals and GenAI engagement choices, with attention to educational inequities that may emerge.
Picture two students working on a difficult assignment, due soon, with a Generative AI (GenAI) chatbot open in another tab.
The assignment, the GenAI tool, and the pressure are the same for both students.
But their goals and behavior may diverge widely depending on the meaning they make of the situation.

For one student, the assignment feels disconnected from the things she really cares about, and the difficulty of the assignment seems to prove that she was never going to be good at this subject anyway.
But the deadline is tight, and she is concerned about her grade.
When schoolwork feels like a performance to survive rather than a challenge to learn from, a rational goal is to do the minimum necessary to achieve an acceptable outcome.

The impulse to do the minimum on assignments is as old as school itself, but the advent of GenAI offers a faster, more fluent, and more successful looking way to achieve this goal than has ever been available before.
As one student put it, "It was a psych pre-class quiz that I had to do and it was due at 11:59 and I had left it to the last minute.
So I decided that an AI tool would be best to make sure I got credit."
(U.S. undergraduate student; [authors], 2026).

The relief that comes with handing in an assignment this way reinforces the usefulness of the approach, and the next time a student is faced with the same choice, it may feel even easier to offload their critical thinking onto GenAI.
For the second student, the same difficulty carries a different meaning: it feels like a challenge she can work through and learn from, instead of like a chore that proves her lack of ability.
She, too, opens the chatbot and begins by asking a question.
The chatbot's explanation makes sense, but it raises more questions, and the problem becomes more interesting.
Somewhere along the way, the exchange stops being about simply finishing the assignment, and instead becomes about learning and understanding.
She asks why an idea works.
She pushes back when an answer seems too simple.
She asks for an example from a primary source, then follows up with her own question that the assignment never mentioned.
Another student described working this way: "I would first try the problem myself, then check my approach...

If I got stuck, I asked [the chatbot] to guide me step-bystep rather than giving the final answer … I actually felt more confident solving similar problems on my own afterward" (U.S. 9th grader; [authors], 2026).
text.formatted: If I got stuck, I asked [the chatbot] to guide me step-bystep rather than giving the final answer … I actually felt more confident solving similar problems on my own afterward" (U.S. 9th grader; <ref type="bibr">[authors], 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Instead of relief, this student is reinforced by mastery: she now understands the steps much better, can catch her own mistakes, and the next hard problem feels like hers to solve.
These two students are not separate archetypes.

When we asked college students about their GenAI use over the past month, the same students who reported asking follow-up questions and requesting push back on their ideas in one context also reported having GenAI produce most or all of an assignment in other contexts ( [authors], 2026).
text.formatted: When we asked college students about their GenAI use over the past month, the same students who reported asking follow-up questions and requesting push back on their ideas in one context also reported having GenAI produce most or all of an assignment in other contexts ( <ref type="bibr">[authors], 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Thus, there is nuanced use within individuals, which also includes nuances behind choices to not use GenAI: to learn independently, avoid accusations of cheating, or because the costs are considered not worthwhile (e.g., environmental costs of data centers, privacy issues).
As educators, we want students to become effective learners capable of leveraging the resources at their disposal.
We often look to the quality of students' work as evidence of what they have learned.
But with GenAI, high-quality work can result from students working through ideas with it or asking it to produce answers for them.
Educators naturally wonder: do students learn when they use GenAI?

This question has led to hundreds of observational and experimental studies, meta-analyses, and meta-analyses of metaanalyses evaluating the outcomes of different amounts of GenAI use (e.g., Emslander et al., 2026).
text.formatted: This question has led to hundreds of observational and experimental studies, meta-analyses, and meta-analyses of metaanalyses evaluating the outcomes of different amounts of GenAI use (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">Emslander et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: But GenAI is not an intervention that adults can apply to, or withhold from, students.
It is a tool already in their lives.
Students make choices about using GenAI every day, whether anyone is scaffolding the development of that decision-making capacity or not.

And testing GenAI access as an intervention evaluates whether a particular tool, with its guardrails, used by students with their own goals, motivation, and skills, is effective for a particular task.

It is not informative about what students learn when they are taught how to use GenAI well, given the opportunity to practice across years, and supported in developing the judgment to know when it is and is not a useful tool.

Studying GenAI outside the context of students' real use will limit our understanding of the thoughts, feelings, behaviors, and environments that shape students' use of it, and thus our ability to help students become effective GenAI users.

We propose broadening the study of AI-in-education to ask: what cultures, contexts, and learning experiences give students the knowledge, skills, beliefs, and motivation to become effective users of GenAI -and do so equitably?

We define an effective user of GenAI as having the capacity to: • know how, when, and when not to use GenAI, evaluated against where the technology is currently reliable and where it fails; • match GenAI use or nonuse to the goal for the current task and situation; • use GenAI to enhance thinking, learning, and work.

This definition is an addition to existing AI literacy frameworks, which have focused on students' understanding of what GenAI is, how to use it and evaluate its output, and what ethical use requires (Feng & Carolus, 2026).
text.formatted: This definition is an addition to existing AI literacy frameworks, which have focused on students' understanding of what GenAI is, how to use it and evaluate its output, and what ethical use requires <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">(Feng & Carolus, 2026)</ref>.

text.text: While these skills are clearly important, we believe equal attention should be paid to the contexts, beliefs, and goals that drive students' choices about GenAI.
A student can be taught how to prompt and still use GenAI to avoid thinking.
She can know that output should be checked and still defer to it when she doubts her judgment.
She can understand responsible use and still avoid the tool because she fears being accused of cheating.
In each case the student has the knowledge.
We argue that what differs is the goals she is striving to meet and the contexts that give rise to those goals.
We make two clarifying notes about this definition.

First, knowing how to use GenAI includes understanding how GenAI works and how to prompt well, as well as how to effectively elicit help that builds learning (i.e., instrumental help-seeking; Roll et al., 2011) and apply effective self-regulated learning strategies to enhance thinking and learning (Zimmerman, 1990).
text.formatted: First, knowing how to use GenAI includes understanding how GenAI works and how to prompt well, as well as how to effectively elicit help that builds learning (i.e., instrumental help-seeking; <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">Roll et al., 2011)</ref> and apply effective self-regulated learning strategies to enhance thinking and learning <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">(Zimmerman, 1990)</ref>.

text.text: Second, although within education contexts the desired goal is learning, not all environments motivate young people to hold learning goals.
In environments that motivate non-learning goals, such as completing work quickly, delegating the work to GenAI becomes a rational choice.
Thus, the study of effective GenAI use for learning requires studying use within contexts that motivate learning goals.
We expand on these points within our motivational model of GenAI engagement.
Drawing on decades of research on the science of learning, development, and motivation, we propose a motivational model of GenAI engagement to organize the research space on GenAI and learning.
Figure 1 provides an overview of this domain-general decision-making process.
text.formatted: Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1</ref> provides an overview of this domain-general decision-making process.

text.text: Our model accounts for how learning environments and students' perceptions of them shape their goals and choices.
Students appraise their situations, form their goals, choose strategies, and accumulate knowledge and experiences that shape their engagement the next time (Walton & Wilson, 2018).
text.formatted: Students appraise their situations, form their goals, choose strategies, and accumulate knowledge and experiences that shape their engagement the next time <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">(Walton & Wilson, 2018)</ref>.

text.text: Set against this model, many AI-ineducation studies focus on a narrow slice of the decision-making process: students' GenAI use and its consequences, often with access assigned rather than chosen (Emslander et al., 2026).
text.formatted: Set against this model, many AI-ineducation studies focus on a narrow slice of the decision-making process: students' GenAI use and its consequences, often with access assigned rather than chosen <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(Emslander et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: In contrast, much of what the learning sciences knows about engaging students sits earlier in the sequence, in students' environments (Darling-Hammond et al., 2020), the appraisals they form (Walton & Wilson, 2018), and the goals associated with those appraisals (Muenks et al., 2024).
text.formatted: In contrast, much of what the learning sciences knows about engaging students sits earlier in the sequence, in students' environments <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Darling-Hammond et al., 2020)</ref>, the appraisals they form <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">(Walton & Wilson, 2018)</ref>, and the goals associated with those appraisals <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">(Muenks et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Furthermore, the decision-making process varies within students: motivational states, including goals, form and shift from situation to situation (Törmänen et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Furthermore, the decision-making process varies within students: motivational states, including goals, form and shift from situation to situation <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">(Törmänen et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: By skipping straight to GenAI use and its outcomes, we skip the processes that produce these behaviors, and students appear as products of GenAI use rather than agents directing a resource.
Strategies.
Many well-known resource-use strategies map onto newer terms commonly used to describe students' use of GenAI.
For example, students such as the one in the second vignette above may seek instrumental help (Roll et al., 2011) by asking for limited assistance so they can solve the problem on their own.
text.formatted: For example, students such as the one in the second vignette above may seek instrumental help <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">(Roll et al., 2011)</ref> by asking for limited assistance so they can solve the problem on their own.

text.text: Instrumental help can include use of GenAI to amplify thinking by (a) aiding learning rather than providing answers, and (b) pushing thinking beyond what is possible on one's own.
Students such as the one in the first vignette may seek executive help from GenAI by asking for answers and solutions, also referred to as offloading or delegating thinking.
Students may also avoid help-seeking entirely (from GenAI or otherwise) to maximize independent learning or because admitting to needing help seems threatening (Karabenick & Dembo, 2011).
text.formatted: Students may also avoid help-seeking entirely (from GenAI or otherwise) to maximize independent learning or because admitting to needing help seems threatening <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">(Karabenick & Dembo, 2011)</ref>.

text.text: Students may even purposefully choose not to use GenAI in situations where other resources (such as a textbook, a peer, their class notes, etc.) would better serve their goals (Chen et al., 2017).
text.formatted: Students may even purposefully choose not to use GenAI in situations where other resources (such as a textbook, a peer, their class notes, etc.) would better serve their goals <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Chen et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: Students move among all four of these resource-use strategies from task to task.
Students' strategies follow from their goals.
Decisions about using GenAI and other educational resources, such as tutors, textbooks, and peer study groups, can be seen as rational strategies designed to achieve specific goals.
Drawing on research on learning and motivation, we distinguish four goal types that shape students' behavior: 1.

Learning goals: Driven by safety, value, and curiosity, a learning goal seeks to build understanding, improvement, and competence in the subject matter (Dweck & Leggett, 1988; Elliot & McGregor, 2001).
text.formatted: Learning goals: Driven by safety, value, and curiosity, a learning goal seeks to build understanding, improvement, and competence in the subject matter <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Dweck & Leggett, 1988;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">Elliot & McGregor, 2001)</ref>.

text.text: Achievement (Performance): Driven by evaluative and high-stakes cues, an achievement goal seeks to demonstrate competence and secure a valued outcome, such as a high score or good grade (Elliot & McGregor, 2001; Elliot et al., 2011; Senko et al., 2011; Sievers et al., 2026).
text.formatted: Achievement (Performance): Driven by evaluative and high-stakes cues, an achievement goal seeks to demonstrate competence and secure a valued outcome, such as a high score or good grade <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(Elliot & McGregor, 2001;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">Elliot et al., 2011;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">Senko et al., 2011;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">Sievers et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Driven by high cost/low value, a completion goal is transactional: it aims simply to get the assignment done (Eccles & Wigfield, 2020; Nicholls et al., 1985).
text.formatted: Driven by high cost/low value, a completion goal is transactional: it aims simply to get the assignment done <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Eccles & Wigfield, 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">Nicholls et al., 1985)</ref>.

text.text: Driven by low safety/low belonging, a protection goal seeks to hide a lack of understanding or avoid the risk of making a mistake (Elliot & McGregor, 2001; Ryan & Pintrich, 1997).
text.formatted: Driven by low safety/low belonging, a protection goal seeks to hide a lack of understanding or avoid the risk of making a mistake <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(Elliot & McGregor, 2001;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">Ryan & Pintrich, 1997)</ref>.

text.text: Each goal is a rational response to the learning environment that a given student inhabits.
Evaluation structures that reward demonstrated ability make achievement goals rational (Muenks et al., 2020; Senko et al., 2011; Sievers et al., 2026).
text.formatted: Evaluation structures that reward demonstrated ability make achievement goals rational <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">(Muenks et al., 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">Senko et al., 2011;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">Sievers et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Classrooms where struggle feels unsafe can make protection rational: students are more likely to avoid seeking help they need, or to seek only the kind that ends the task, so they withdraw effort (Karabenick, 2004; Ryan et al., 2001).
text.formatted: Classrooms where struggle feels unsafe can make protection rational: students are more likely to avoid seeking help they need, or to seek only the kind that ends the task, so they withdraw effort <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">(Karabenick, 2004;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">Ryan et al., 2001)</ref>.

text.text: Tasks that demand more effort than they seem worth, or more time than the schedule allows, tend to elicit completion goals (Eccles & Wigfield, 2020).
text.formatted: Tasks that demand more effort than they seem worth, or more time than the schedule allows, tend to elicit completion goals <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Eccles & Wigfield, 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Achievement, completion, and protection goals are all generally well-served by GenAI's fluent generation of believable work products.
In contrast, when students hold learning goals, their objective is to master the knowledge or skill at hand.
Students holding learning goals may also care about outcomes such as earning a good grade or passing a test, but their interest in the topic goes beyond the grade (Grant & Dweck, 2003).
text.formatted: Students holding learning goals may also care about outcomes such as earning a good grade or passing a test, but their interest in the topic goes beyond the grade <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">(Grant & Dweck, 2003)</ref>.

text.text: We therefore predict that students holding learning goals will tend to use GenAI to enhance, rather than offload, their critical thinking.
Goals do not follow directly from the objective features of a task.
Instead, they are determined by what those features mean to the student in a given moment.
These meaning-making processes, or appraisals, are what create a situation's motivational consequences for each person (Eccles & Wigfield, 2020).
text.formatted: These meaning-making processes, or appraisals, are what create a situation's motivational consequences for each person <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Eccles & Wigfield, 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Faced with the same assignment, a student may judge that she can succeed, that the task is worth the effort, that it is safe to struggle or ask for help, and that her own judgment matters -or she may reach the opposite conclusions.
These appraisals are situation-specific rather than fixed properties of individual students (Törmänen et al., 2025).
text.formatted: These appraisals are situation-specific rather than fixed properties of individual students <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">(Törmänen et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Expectations for success vary across activities and contexts (Eccles & Wigfield, 2020) and may shift as competing demands change (Beymer et al., 2026).
text.formatted: Expectations for success vary across activities and contexts <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Eccles & Wigfield, 2020)</ref> and may shift as competing demands change <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Beymer et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Concerns about safety and belonging may rise and fall according to identity-relevant cues in the setting (Kroeper et al., 2026).
text.formatted: Concerns about safety and belonging may rise and fall according to identity-relevant cues in the setting <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">(Kroeper et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Task value is also malleable: helping students connect course material to their lives increases interest and grades, particularly among students with low expectations for success (Hulleman & Harackiewicz, 2009).
text.formatted: Task value is also malleable: helping students connect course material to their lives increases interest and grades, particularly among students with low expectations for success <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">(Hulleman & Harackiewicz, 2009)</ref>.

text.text: Thus, the situation itself does not determine a student's goal directly.
Instead, students engage in complex meaning-making processes, taking into account a variety of environmental cues and relevant beliefs, which together make some goals more salient than others.
The learning environment shapes appraisals by providing cues about what and who is valued.

Stereotypes about who has valuable abilities can undermine belonging (Bauer et al., 2025), while features of the task and setting shape whether students see the work as valuable (Eccles & Wigfield, 2020).
text.formatted: Stereotypes about who has valuable abilities can undermine belonging <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Bauer et al., 2025)</ref>, while features of the task and setting shape whether students see the work as valuable <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Eccles & Wigfield, 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Furthermore, many students are attuned to cues that their gender, racial/ethnic background, or their family's immigrant status or socio-economic background may be devalued in a given setting, a vigilance that helps them navigate the context (Kroeper et al., 2026).
text.formatted: Furthermore, many students are attuned to cues that their gender, racial/ethnic background, or their family's immigrant status or socio-economic background may be devalued in a given setting, a vigilance that helps them navigate the context <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">(Kroeper et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Students facing such cues may feel the need to work even harder to prove themselves, or may disengage from school or from the subject matter if they believe their effort is futile.
For example, computing has long been seen as a field in which men belong and excel (Master et al., 2025).
text.formatted: For example, computing has long been seen as a field in which men belong and excel <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">(Master et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Young women may avoid new technology for fear that being "techie" is not for "people like me."
When the learning environment sends signals that students are at risk of being judged negatively, it brings out threat appraisals and protection goals.
Considering the motivational process model as a whole, it bears mentioning that no goal is inherently good or problematic.
Adults routinely delegate or offload mundane tasks to preserve effort for more valuable work (Zhu et al., 2026).
text.formatted: Adults routinely delegate or offload mundane tasks to preserve effort for more valuable work <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">(Zhu et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Self-protection in a threatening environment may be critical to a student's well-being (Kroeper et al., 2026).
text.formatted: Self-protection in a threatening environment may be critical to a student's well-being <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">(Kroeper et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: What educators perceive as a student problem is often a mismatch between the educator's goal to assess learning, and the goal the environment has made rational for the student.
Place the same student in three different environments, and three different goals with three different strategies for GenAI use may emerge.

Each choice that a given student makes about GenAI use builds knowledge and experience that shapes the next appraisal, allowing small task-level consequences to accumulate into trajectories of skill, confidence, agency, and belonging.
This recursive process, each experience shaping how the next situation is interpreted and approached, is what makes the model developmental rather than a snapshot (Walton & Wilson, 2018).
text.formatted: This recursive process, each experience shaping how the next situation is interpreted and approached, is what makes the model developmental rather than a snapshot <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">(Walton & Wilson, 2018)</ref>.

text.text: So far, we have focused on motivational processes that are by and large unchanged from the pre-GenAI era.
While GenAI is a new resource with new affordances, the basic processes by which students navigate resources in their learning environment are not new.
However, GenAI does introduce unique affordances to that environment which we believe are likely to shape student motivation in the years to come.
In this section, we discuss the implications of some of these affordances for educational research and policy.
Even when students hold learning goals, it does not necessarily follow that they will use GenAI (or other learning resources) effectively.
Strategically selecting which resources to use for learning has always been a challenge, even before GenAI.

For example, college undergraduates benefited from an intervention prompting them to plan proactively what resources they would use for studying; e.g., reviewing lecture notes, attending office hours, and consulting with peers (Chen et al., 2017).
text.formatted: For example, college undergraduates benefited from an intervention prompting them to plan proactively what resources they would use for studying; e.g., reviewing lecture notes, attending office hours, and consulting with peers <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Chen et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: GenAI adds a new learning resource to the mix.

A student who chooses GenAI as a learning resource must know how to use it effectively to elicit instrumental help (Roll et al., 2011).  (Aleven et al., 2003), but they can be taught: when students were given metacognitive feedback on their helpseeking, they improved their help-seeking skills and those improvements carried into new material a month after the support was withdrawn (Roll et al., 2011).
text.formatted: A student who chooses GenAI as a learning resource must know how to use it effectively to elicit instrumental help <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">(Roll et al., 2011)</ref>.  <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Aleven et al., 2003)</ref>, but they can be taught: when students were given metacognitive feedback on their helpseeking, they improved their help-seeking skills and those improvements carried into new material a month after the support was withdrawn <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">(Roll et al., 2011)</ref>.

text.text: Historically, schools have rarely engaged in teaching these competencies (Karabenick & Dembo, 2011), relying instead on adults to tell young people which resources to use, sequence hints for them, and withhold the answers to check for understanding.
text.formatted: Historically, schools have rarely engaged in teaching these competencies <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">(Karabenick & Dembo, 2011)</ref>, relying instead on adults to tell young people which resources to use, sequence hints for them, and withhold the answers to check for understanding.

text.text: With the addition of GenAI, adults have less control over the availability of hints, correct answers, and resources than they did in the past.
Therefore, 21 st century schools need to teach students the skills of seeking help effectively and monitoring their own learning progress more explicitly than was previously necessary.
Unlike previous technologies, GenAI participates in meaning-making.

It introduces questions, offers pushback, and contributes to the knowledge a student is building, requiring students to adopt a trust-but-verify stance by critically reviewing outputs, checking sources, and evaluating plausibility against their own understanding (Wu et al., 2025).
text.formatted: It introduces questions, offers pushback, and contributes to the knowledge a student is building, requiring students to adopt a trust-but-verify stance by critically reviewing outputs, checking sources, and evaluating plausibility against their own understanding <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">(Wu et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Yet students may experience this highly intelligent meaning-making partner the way they were taught to experience other authorities in their lives.
Children learn early whether it is appropriate to question or seek help from authority figures, and those lessons differ by social class (Calarco, 2014).
text.formatted: Children learn early whether it is appropriate to question or seek help from authority figures, and those lessons differ by social class <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Calarco, 2014)</ref>.

text.text: Faced with the question: "Is my thinking worth contributing?"
a student whose voice was never valued is unlikely to feel ownership now.
Becoming an effective GenAI user depends on learning environments that foster authority and ownership.

Classrooms that create a climate of respect and belonging, and that value learning over getting the right answer, build students' authority over their ideas and reduce their worry about being judged for sharing them (Engle & Conant, 2002; Muenks et al., 2020).
text.formatted: Classrooms that create a climate of respect and belonging, and that value learning over getting the right answer, build students' authority over their ideas and reduce their worry about being judged for sharing them <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">(Engle & Conant, 2002;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">Muenks et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Those conditions, however, are set by adults still working out an unfamiliar technology for themselves.

A natural reaction to a technology we do not fully understand is to reach for control, either by holding students to high standards without giving them the support to meet them, or by lowering the demands and blocking the tool (Yeager et al., in press).
text.formatted: A natural reaction to a technology we do not fully understand is to reach for control, either by holding students to high standards without giving them the support to meet them, or by lowering the demands and blocking the tool <ref type="bibr">(Yeager et al., in press)</ref>.

text.text: Both approaches limit student agency and focus more on detecting or banning use.

In contrast, a "mentor mindset" can hold students to high standards while providing the support needed for students to safely fail, learn from mistakes, and build their skill, confidence, and ownership of judgment (Yeager et al., in press).
text.formatted: In contrast, a "mentor mindset" can hold students to high standards while providing the support needed for students to safely fail, learn from mistakes, and build their skill, confidence, and ownership of judgment <ref type="bibr">(Yeager et al., in press)</ref>.

text.text: Knowing that GenAI output should be checked is not enough; students need to be shown that their judgment is valued.
Effective GenAI use also requires a working map of where the tool is currently reliable and where it fails.
This boundary is often described as a "jagged edge" because it is counterintuitive and constantly shifting (Dell'Acqua et al., 2026).
text.formatted: This boundary is often described as a "jagged edge" because it is counterintuitive and constantly shifting <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Dell'Acqua et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: No fixed playbook can therefore replace calibrated experience.
Students need structured opportunities to test the tool against tasks they understand, to watch it succeed and fail, and to update their mental representations.

This practice works best when the learning environment communicates that (a) everyone can become an effective user of GenAI, and (b) trying and learning from mistakes is valued over performance outcomes.
This presumes schools permit GenAI use.

In our 2026 national adolescent data, 42% of students whose parents did not have a college degree attended schools where GenAI use was prohibited, compared with 17% of students with college-educated parents ( [authors], 2026).
text.formatted: In our 2026 national adolescent data, 42% of students whose parents did not have a college degree attended schools where GenAI use was prohibited, compared with 17% of students with college-educated parents ( <ref type="bibr">[authors]</ref>, 2026).

text.text: Permitting practice for some students and not others is how the next digital divide gets built (Capraro et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Permitting practice for some students and not others is how the next digital divide gets built <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Capraro et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Teachers need the same opportunity.
Whether they are using GenAI to generate lesson plans, teaching about GenAI, or simply enforcing GenAI policy, teachers cannot support a judgment they have not had the chance to build.
Time, space, and support for teachers' productive tinkering must be a high priority.
Fortunately, learning environments can be changed at scale through providing teachers with structured, supported practice (Yeager et al., in press).
text.formatted: Fortunately, learning environments can be changed at scale through providing teachers with structured, supported practice <ref type="bibr">(Yeager et al., in press)</ref>.

text.text: Drawing on decades of motivation and help-seeking research, we have argued that research must study much more than the overall frequency of students' GenAI use, or whether students use GenAI to offload their critical thinking.
How students choose to engage in learning follows from their appraisals of the learning environment, the goals those appraisals make salient, and the strategies that rationally follow those goals.
To learn how to support effective GenAI use, research and policy must seek to understand these beliefs and motivations.
When young people see the purpose of the material they are learning, finishing quickly with minimal effort is no longer the rational goal.
If it feels safe to struggle and make mistakes, difficulty stops indicating inability, and students feel more empowered to hand in work that reflects their real, imperfect learning.
And when students are treated as autonomous individuals with agency, whose judgment is respected, then they have a reason to believe their judgment is worth using.
Each of these experiences, and many more, may create learning environments that support young people to use GenAI
This work was supported by a National Science Foundation grant (2201928).
text.formatted: This work was supported by a <rs type="funder">National Science Foundation</rs> grant (<rs type="grantNumber">2201928</rs>).

text.text: Figure 1 A Motivational Model of GenAI Engagement recognize what she does not yet understand, ask for an explanation rather than an answer, judge what comes back against what she already knows, and decide what to do next.
Students do not become skilled help-seekers on their own effectively over time.

Thus, our model organizes the research space around these experiences by naming key ideas and pointing to the development of measures, hypotheses, and research designs surrounding the question the field now needs to answer: what cultures, contexts, and learning experiences give students the knowledge, skills, beliefs, and motivation to become effective users of GenAI, and do so equitably?

To answer such questions, research must measure key aspects of the learning environment, students' beliefs, appraisals, and goals, and the strategies they use to achieve these goals, not just their overall amount of GenAI use.

We call for research designs that vary the signals the learning environment sends about what is valued, such as how assignments are designed and graded, and then examine how students' goals and behavior with GenAI shift in response to these changes.
Studies examining students' GenAI use will benefit from collecting data to understand why students make the choices they do.

Measures of the whole processsituation, appraisal, goal, strategy, consequence -will allow the field to learn what supports effective GenAI use among different student populations and scale the most effective approaches.
Powerful narratives are emerging in popular culture that frame GenAI as a miracle tutor on the one hand, or as a source of cognitive decay on the other.
But if our policies are to be based on evidence, then science must catch up with these narratives.
We hope this model helps the science set the pace by identifying the kinds of factors that lead students to become effective GenAI users rather than refereeing the tool.
What we want for students has not changed.

Before GenAI, the science of learning and development sought to develop young people who pose questions, seek out resources to answer them, evaluate what they find across multiple sources and perspectives, and work toward goals that matter (Learning Policy Institute & Turnaround for Children, 2021).
text.formatted: Before GenAI, the science of learning and development sought to develop young people who pose questions, seek out resources to answer them, evaluate what they find across multiple sources and perspectives, and work toward goals that matter (Learning Policy Institute & Turnaround for Children, 2021).

text.text: GenAI has changed the conditions for getting there.
The work ahead is building classrooms where the rational choice and the learning choice are the same choice -for every student.
